t: Minimum Operations to Convert Number — BFS on a 1001-State Implicit Graph
o: Starting from x = start (guaranteed in [0, 1000]), each operation replaces x by x + nums[i], x - nums[i] or x XOR nums[i] — but only while 0 <= x <= 1000. An operation MAY push x outside that window, after which x is frozen forever. Convert start into goal (which may be huge or negative — Example 2 reaches -4) in the fewest operations, or return -1 as in Example 3, where 0 can never become 1. Example 1 needs two ops: 2 -> 14 (+12) -> 12 (-2). The decisive observation: only the 1001 in-range values are ever expandable states, so this is a shortest-path problem on a tiny implicit graph with unit-weight edges — BFS explores level by level and the first arrival at goal is optimal.
k: Model values 0..1000 as graph nodes and the three operations per num as unit edges; minimum operations = shortest path distance.
Out-of-range neighbors matter ONLY when they equal goal (final move); enqueueing them would explode the state space for no benefit.
Mark visited states on enqueue: <= 1001 states times 3 x |nums| candidate edges bounds BFS to about 3e6 steps.
Detect goal when GENERATING neighbors, not only when popping: an out-of-range goal can never enter the queue.

a.i: Run standard BFS from start over the implicit graph. For each dequeued x (always in range), try every num under all three operations; if a neighbor equals goal return the current distance plus one, otherwise enqueue it if it stays in range and has not been seen.
s: Seed the queue with start and its distance 0.
Dequeue x and iterate nums, generating x + v, x - v, x ^ v.
If any generated value equals goal, return dist(x) + 1 immediately.
Otherwise enqueue in-range unseen neighbors with their new distances.
If the queue empties, goal is unreachable: return -1.
a.t: O(3 · S · |nums|) with S <= 1001 expandable states — well under 3e6 edge relaxations even for |nums| = 1000.
a.sp: O(S) — the visited/distance table plus the queue of in-range values.

a.n: Approach 2: Dijkstra with a Priority Queue
a.i: The same graph solved with lazy Dijkstra: pop the closest unfinished state, skip stale entries, and relax the three outgoing edges per num. With unit weights this is strictly heavier than BFS, but the pattern generalizes directly to weighted operation costs, making it the template worth knowing for follow-ups. Treat goal as an ordinary node that may live outside [0, 1000]: only edges INTO it bypass the range check.
s: Initialize dist[start] = 0 and push (0, start) onto a min-heap.
Pop the smallest entry (d, x); if x equals goal return d.
Skip stale entries where d exceeds the recorded best distance.
Relax x ± v and x ^ v: allow neighbors equal to goal or inside [0, 1000], pushing improved distances.
a.t: O(E log V) with E ≈ 3 · |nums| · S and V <= 1002 nodes — asymptotically worse than BFS here since every edge weighs 1.
a.sp: O(V + E) — the distance map plus the heap.

w: BFS is the right answer in an interview; mention Dijkstra only when asked how the model extends to weighted operations. Pitfalls: enqueueing out-of-range values (dead ends that bloat memory), checking goal solely at dequeue time (out-of-range goals can never be enqueued), forgetting XOR as the third operation, and operating on out-of-range x (the rules forbid it). Edge cases: goal reached in one move from start, unreachable goals (Example 3's parity-style dead end), and large |nums| making the visited-set bound the runtime. Follow-up: weighted operations favor Dijkstra; bidirectional BFS also works because +v, -v and XOR are all self-invertible.
